claims.label: Breach of Quiet Enjoyment / Constructive Eviction
claims.note: Fact-intensive claim, informed by comparable cases rather than a formula -- see cited cases.

claims.label: Breach of Implied Warranty of Suitability
claims.note: California follows the majority "caveat lessee" rule for commercial tenancies -- courts have generally declined to extend the residential implied warranty of habitability to commercial leases (commercial tenants are treated as sophisticated parties expected to negotiate their own express repair/condition covenants). Texas's implied warranty of SUITABILITY (a distinct, narrower doctrine -- Davidow v. Inwood North Professional Group-Phase I, 747 S.W.2d 373 (Tex. 1988)) is the only jurisdiction confirmed here to recognize an implied-warranty theory for commercial premises at all. Absent confirmed recognition of an implied warranty in this state, treat this theory as a longshot and look instead to the lease's own express repair/maintenance covenants and the Breach of Quiet Enjoyment claim above. If breach is found, recovery (or the amount of rent excused) tends to track close to the amount actually withheld or spent, since it's usually a dollar-for-dollar rent abatement or an invoiced repair cost -- discounted here only for the chance a court finds the premises only partially unsuitable. No citation-backed damages ratio identified beyond that; treat the low end as a modeling heuristic.

claims.label: Attorney's Fees
claims.note: Posture-tiered flat-dollar estimate (went to trial) -- fees are driven by procedural effort, not claim size, for a typical matter in this range; a large or unusually complex matter can run higher.

extractedFacts.wrongfulLockoutCitation: CORRECTED (round-2 research): Cal. Civ. Code Sec. 789.3's $100/day statutory penalty applies, by its own express terms, only to property 'used by a tenant as his or her residence' -- it does not reach commercial tenancies. Commercial self-help lockouts in California are instead governed by the common-law/Code Civ. Proc. Sec. 1159-1161 framework confirmed in Jordan v. Talbot, 55 Cal. 2d 597 (1961): a lease right-of-re-entry clause may be enforced only through judicial process, and a clause purporting to authorize forcible self-help is void as against public policy. That framework yields ACTUAL damages only, not a statutory per-diem penalty.

outcome.description: The jury found the landlord liable for premises liability and negligence (no liability for concealment), awarded the tenant $144,300 in lost profits and $77,700 in other past economic loss ($222,000), and found the tenant's unpaid rent caused the landlord no harm on the cross-complaint. The trial court then granted JNOV for the landlord under the lease's limitation-of-liability clause. The Court of Appeal reversed the JNOV (the clause is invalid under Civil Code section 1668 as applied to the Health and Safety Code disclosure violations, and the indemnity clause does not reach gross negligence), affirmed the denial of the landlord's partial JNOV on the $77,700, and remanded.
outcome.finalNote: JNOV reversed and the $222,000 verdict upheld against the damages challenge; on remand the landlord may still ask the trial court to rule on its alternative new-trial motion, which had been denied as moot.
